title: Vector Quantities in Mechanics
short_intro: Vector quantities are physical observables possessing both magnitude and direction that obey the parallelogram law of vector addition. In classical mechanics, kinematics and dynamics are formulated using vectors to describe spatial translation, rotation, and forces acting on continuous media and point masses.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of scalars and vectors, graphical representation, unit vectors, position vector, resolution of vectors in 2D and 3D Cartesian coordinates, dot and cross products, directional cosines, and basic applications to displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Vector differential operators (gradient, divergence, curl), conservative fields, central forces, pseudo-vectors (axial vectors like angular momentum, torque, Coriolis force), coordinate transformations, and invariance under rotation.

prerequisites: Concept of scalar quantities and dimensions

concept_notes.heading: Classification of Physical Quantities
bullets: Scalars are completely specified by a magnitude with appropriate units, following ordinary algebraic laws (e.g., mass, time, temperature, work, energy).

Vectors require magnitude, direction, and specific spatial orientation, transforming under coordinate rotation according to linear transformation rules (e.g., displacement, velocity, force, momentum).
Tensors of rank zero are scalars, rank one are vectors, and higher ranks describe complex physical phenomena such as stress, strain, and moments of inertia.

concept_notes.heading: Polar versus Axial (Pseudo) Vectors
bullets: Polar vectors represent linear translation and have a natural sense of direction associated with spatial displacement, reversing sign under spatial inversion (parity transformation r → -r). Examples include linear velocity, acceleration, and force.

Axial vectors (pseudo-vectors) represent rotational characteristics and are associated with a rotation axis. They do not invert their direction under spatial inversion (r → -r), retaining their sign because they are defined via cross products of two polar vectors.
Examples of axial vectors include angular momentum (L = r × p), torque (τ = r × F), magnetic field, and the Coriolis force in rotating reference frames.

concept_notes.heading: Algebraic Operations on Vectors
bullets: Vector addition is commutative (A + B = B + A) and associative, performed graphically via the triangle or parallelogram law, or analytically via component-wise addition.
Scalar (dot) product yields a scalar quantity representing the projection of one vector onto another: A · B = AB cos(θ), obeying distributive laws.
Vector (cross) product yields an axial vector perpendicular to the plane containing the operands: A × B = AB sin(θ)n^, obeying anti-commutativity (A × B = -B × A).

concept_notes.heading: Differentiation and Integration of Vectors
bullets: A vector function r(t) depends on a scalar parameter such as time t, representing a curve in space traced by the tip of the vector.
The time derivative of a vector function yields its rate of change, evaluated by differentiating its Cartesian components: dr/dt = (dx/dt)i^ + (dy/dt)j^ + (dz/dt)k^.
Product rules apply to vector derivatives, such as d/dt(A · B) = (dA/dt) · B + A · (dB/dt) and d/dt(A × B) = (dA/dt) × B + A × (dB/dt).

derivations.title: Magnitude and Direction of Resultant Vector via Parallelogram Law
derivations.conditions: Two vectors P and Q acting at an angle θ relative to each other.
steps: Construct a parallelogram with adjacent sides representing vectors P and Q, with the angle between their tails equal to θ.
Drop a perpendicular from the head of vector Q to the extended line of vector P, forming a right-angled triangle.
Using Pythagoras theorem on the large right-angled triangle, the square of the resultant magnitude R² = (P + Q cos(θ))² + (Q sin(θ))².
Expand the binomial: R² = P² + 2PQ cos(θ) + Q² cos²(θ) + Q² sin²(θ) = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos(θ).
For direction angle α made by R with vector P, use trigonometry: tan(α) = (Q sin(θ)) / (P + Q cos(θ)).

derivations.title: Time Derivative of a Unit Vector with Constant Magnitude
derivations.conditions: A unit vector n^(t) rotating in a plane with angular velocity ω = dθ/dt.
steps: Express the unit vector in terms of polar coordinates in a plane: n^(t) = \cos(\theta) i^ + \sin(\theta) j^.
Differentiate with respect to time t using the chain rule: dn^/dt = -\sin(\theta) (d\theta/dt) i^ + \cos(\theta) (d\theta/dt) j^.
Substitute dθ/dt = ω and factor out ω: dn^/dt = \omega (-\sin(\theta) i^ + \cos(\theta) j^).
Observe that the vector (-sin(θ)i^ + cos(θ)j^) is perpendicular to n^(t), pointing in the direction of increasing θ.
Represent this geometrically as dn^/dt = \omega \times n^, where ω is the angular velocity vector perpendicular to the plane of rotation.

formula_sheet.name: Scalar Dot Product
formula_sheet.equation_html: \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z = AB \cos(\theta)
formula_sheet.variables: A, B = Vector magnitudes, θ = Angle between vectors

formula_sheet.name: Vector Cross Product
formula_sheet.equation_html: \vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} i^ & j^ & k^ \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix}
formula_sheet.variables: A_x, A_y, A_z and B_x, B_y, B_z = Cartesian components

formula_sheet.name: Position Vector
formula_sheet.equation_html: \vec{r} = x i^ + y j^ + z k^

formula_sheet.name: Direction Cosines
formula_sheet.variables: l, m, n = Direction cosines; α, β, γ = Angles with axes
formula_sheet.conditions: Non-zero vector A; l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1

formula_sheet.name: Angular Momentum Vector
formula_sheet.variables: r = Position vector, p = Linear momentum, m = Mass, v = Velocity
formula_sheet.conditions: Evaluated about a specific origin point

formula_sheet.name: Central Force Vector
formula_sheet.variables: f(r) = Magnitude function of distance r, r^ = Radial unit vector
formula_sheet.conditions: Force acts along the line joining the center and the particle

formula_sheet.name: Coriolis Force Vector
formula_sheet.variables: m = Mass, ω = Angular velocity of rotating frame, v_r = Relative velocity

formula_sheet.name: Gravitational Force Vector
formula_sheet.variables: G = Universal gravitational constant, r_12 = Displacement vector from mass 1 to mass 2
formula_sheet.conditions: Point masses separated by distance r

graphs_and_experiments.title: Parallelogram Law of Vector Addition Graphical Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two vectors A and B originating from a common point, completed into a parallelogram with the diagonal representing the resultant vector R = A + B.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that vector addition is geometric composition independent of coordinate choice, showing the dependence of the resultant magnitude on the included angle θ.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in finding maximum and minimum resultants when vectors act in the same or opposite directions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resolution of a Vector into Rectangular Components
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A vector r in the X-Y plane with projections along the X and Y axes forming a right triangle with angle θ relative to the X-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates orthogonal decomposition where r_x = r cos(θ) and r_y = r sin(θ), enabling algebraic manipulation of multidimensional vectors.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly applied in resolving inclined plane forces, projectile motion velocity components, and equilibrium problems.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cross Product Right-Hand Rule Visualization
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Vectors A and B drawn from a common origin spanning a plane, with the cross product vector C perpendicular to the plane pointing upward according to right-hand curl.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the non-coplanar axial nature of vector products, essential for defining torque, angular momentum, and magnetic forces.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core conceptual questions in TGT/PGT regarding the direction of torque and angular momentum vectors.

solved_numericals.question: If two vectors A and B have magnitudes 6 units and 8 units respectively, and the angle between them is 60°, find the magnitude of their resultant vector.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for the magnitude of the resultant: R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB \cos(\theta)}.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the angle between two vectors A = 3i^ + 4j^ + 5k^ and B = 3i^ + 4j^ - 5k^.
solution_steps: Compute the dot product A · B = (3)(3) + (4)(4) + (5)(-5) = 9 + 16 - 25 = 0.
Compute the magnitudes: A = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{50} and B = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{50}.
Use the dot product definition: A \cdot B = AB \cos(\theta) \implies 0 = \sqrt{50} \sqrt{50} \cos(\theta).

solved_numericals.question: A particle moves with position vector r(t) = a \cos(\omega t) i^ + a \sin(\omega t) j^. Find its velocity vector and show that velocity is perpendicular to the position vector at any instant t.
solution_steps: Differentiate the position vector with respect to time t: v = dr/dt = d/dt[a \cos(\omega t)] i^ + d/dt[a \sin(\omega t)] j^.
Evaluate derivatives: v = -a\omega \sin(\omega t) i^ + a\omega \cos(\omega t) j^.
Calculate the dot product of position vector r and velocity vector v: r \cdot v = [a \cos(\omega t)][-a\omega \sin(\omega t)] + [a \sin(\omega t)][a\omega \cos(\omega t)].
Simplify the expression: r \cdot v = -a^2 \omega \sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t) + a^2 \omega \sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t) = 0.
Since the dot product is zero, the vectors r and v are perpendicular for all time t.
solved_numericals.answer: v = -a\omega \sin(\omega t) i^ + a\omega \cos(\omega t) j^; r \cdot v = 0 (perpendicular)

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes a flat, three-dimensional Euclidean space where standard linear vector algebra and Cartesian coordinate systems apply.
Limitations arise in general relativity or non-Euclidean spaces where parallel transport of vectors depends on spacetime curvature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Any quantity with magnitude and direction is strictly a vector.
common_misconceptions.correct: A vector must also obey specific coordinate transformation laws (rotation laws), which excludes quantities like finite rotations that do not commute.
common_misconceptions.why: Finite rotations are not vectors because their addition depends on the sequence of operations, whereas infinitesimal rotations do behave as vectors.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The cross product of two vectors is a scalar.
common_misconceptions.correct: The cross product of two polar vectors yields an axial vector (pseudo-vector) perpendicular to their plane.
common_misconceptions.why: The vector product incorporates direction determined by the right-hand rule, distinguishing it from the scalar dot product.

quick_revision: Resultant of two vectors: R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB \cos(\theta)}.
Dot product gives scalar: A \cdot B = AB \cos(\theta); zero for orthogonal vectors.
Cross product gives axial vector: A \times B = AB \sin(\theta) \hat{n}; zero for parallel vectors.
Axial vectors like torque and angular momentum do not invert under spatial inversion.
